Reduced strength of the frontalis muscle (which is located on the forehead).
Incidents in which a piece of food or other objects get stuck in the upper airway and provoke coughing, gagging, inability to talk, and difficulty breathing.
An electromyographic finding associated with erratic or absent neuromuscular transmission with erratic, moment-to-moment changes in the shape of the motor unit potential (MUP).
Recurrent episodes of apnea that are precipitated by factors such as illness, fatigue, or stress.
Compound muscle action potential amplitude (CMAP) facilitation denotes an increase in tendon reflexes, strength, or CMAP amplitude after 10 seconds of maximal voluntary contraction.

The presence of autoantibodies (immunoglobulins) in the blood circulation that react against Ganglioside-monosialic acid (GM1), which is a type of glycosphingolipid with one sialic acid. GM1 is located on the outer layer of the plasma membrane, and plays a vital role in neurogenesis, nerve development, differentiation and repair after injury.
Swelling from fluid accumulation (serous fluid infiltration into the interstitial space) in the cerebellum.
An increased or decreased activity of the mitochondrial respiratory chain.
Bradypnea is referring to breathing that is abnormally slow.
An increase in the level of choline-containing compounds in the brain identified by magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS).

Presence of persistent islands of renal blastema in the postnatal kidney. Nephroblastomatosis represents a complex abnormality of nephrogenesis and has been defined as the persistence of metanephricblastema into infancy and childhood.
Abnormally persistent clusters of embryonal cells, representing microscopic malformations (dysplasias) of the developing kidney.
Naevus flammeus localised in the skin of the eyelid.
Hyperplasia of the islets of Langerhans, i.e., of the regions of the pancreas that contain its endocrine cells.
Abnormal increased size of the viscera of the abdomen.
Underdevelopment of the abdominal musculature.
The presence of a capillary hemangioma, which are hemangiomas with small endothelial spaces.
Macular dystrophy is a nonspecific term for premature retinal cell aging and cell death, generally confied to the macula in which no clear extrinsic cause is evident.
Any abnormality of the alveolar ridges (on the upper or lower jaws). The alveolar ridges contain the sockets (alveoli) of the teeth.
Diminished activity of the enzyme 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase in liver tissue.
Diminished activity of the enzyme 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase in muscle tissue.
Any deviation from the normal concentration of carnitine in the blood circulation.
Abnormally increased levels of lysine in cerebrospinal fluid.
An increased concentration of lysine in the blood.
A form of lactic acidemia that occurs in relation to stress or infection.
A decreased concentration of free (unbound) carnitine in the blood.
An increased concentration of lysine in the urine.
Fat infiltration in the pancreas.
A type of glaucoma defined by an open, normal appearing anterior chamber angle and raised intraocular pressure,
Hemorrhage between the skull and periosteum of a newborn resulting from rupture of blood vessels that cross the periosteum.
Death of cells in the basal ganglia.
High urine phosphate in the presence of hypophosphatemia.
Abnormally increased concentration of hydrogencarbonate in the urine.
An abnormally increased sodium concentration in the urine in the presence of hyponatremia.
An increased concentration of potassium(1+) in the urine.
Excretion in urine of proteins of a size smaller than albumin (molecular weight 69 kD).
Increased height of the wing (or ala) of the ilium (which is the large expanded portion which bounds the greater pelvis laterally).
An abnormally straight configuration of the clavicle, a tubular bone which normally is doubly curved .
Excessive growth (overgrowth) of the facial bones, that is of the facial skeleton.
An accumulation of calcium and phosphate in arteries with mineral deposits in the intimal or medial layer of the vessel wall in the thoracic aorta.
The presence of calcium-containing calculi (stones) in the kidneys.
An abnormally decreased concentration of parathyroid hormone.
An increased concentration of calcifediol in the blood. Calcifediol is also known as 25-hydroxycholecalciferol or 25-Hydroxyvitamin D3.
An increased concentration of calcitriol in the blood. Calcitriol is also known as 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol or 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3.
An elevated level of osteocalcin in the blood.
A abnormal elevation above the normal concentration of beta-C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen in the blood circulation.
Inflammation of the uveal tract in which the primary site of inflammation is the anterior chamber.
Fever that occurs at daily intervals.
Median longitudinal length of the ear more than two standard deviations below the mean in the presence of some, but not all, parts of the normal ear.
An abnormal connection between the gut and another hollow organ, such as the bladder, urethra, vagina, or other regions of the gastrointestinal tract.
An abnormality of the structure of the pulmonary veins.
The presence of a bilobed gallbladder, related to a duplication of the gallbladder primordium.
An abnormality of the pulmonary artery.
An abnormally squared appearance of the bony pelvis, a normally rounded or basin-shaped structure.
The presence of a bicuspid pulmonary valve.
Delayed maturation and calcification of the rami (branches) of the pubic bone.
Bony fusion between the humerus and scapula, leading to an impairment in mobility of the affected shoulder joint.
Schisis (cleft or cleavage) of vertebral bodies.

Axenfeld's anomaly is a bilateral disorder characterized by a prominent, anteriorly displaced Schwalbe's line (posterior embryotoxon) and peripheral iris strands which span the anterior chamber angle to attach to Schwalbe's line.
Increased amount of pigmentation in the fovea centralis.
An increased susceptibility to cutaneous abscess formation, as manifested by a medical history of recurrent cutaneous abscesses.
Urticaria may be caused by cold temperatures.

Molluscum contagiosum is a cutaneous viral infection that is commonly observed in both healthy and immunocompromised children. The infection is caused by a member of the Poxviridae family, the molluscum contagiosum virus. Molluscum contagiosum presents as single or multiple small white or flesh-colored papules that typically have a central umbilication. The central umbilication may be difficult to observe in young children and, instead, may bear an appearance similar to an acneiform eruption. The lesions vary in size (from 1 mm to 1 cm in diameter) and are painless, although a subset of patients report pruritus in the area of infection. On average, 11-20 papules appear on the body during the course of infection and generally remains a self-limiting disease. However, in immunosuppressed patients, molluscum contagiosum can be a severe infection with hundreds of lesions developing on the body. Extensive eruption is indicative of an advanced immunodeficiency state.
A recurrent infection of the GI tract with helicobacter pylori, a gram-negative, microaerophilic bacterium usually found in the stomach.
Slightly raised wart 2-5 mm in diameter often associated with viral infections, commonly persistent in immunodeficient individuals.

Human papillomaviruses (HPVs) are small oncogenic viruses. HPV has been shown to cause a variety of lesions and malignancies, which predominantly affect the anogenital region. Low-risk, non-oncogenic HPV types are associated with anogenital warts and recurrent respiratory papillomatosis while high-risk, oncogenic types are associated with cervical, penile, anal, vaginal, vulvar, and oropharyngeal cancers. Infection with anogenital HPV is usually asymptomatic and resolves spontaneously without consequences in the immunocompetent host. When disease does occur, the most common manifestation is genital warts, which may be small papules, or flat, smooth or pedunculated lesions. This resolution of HPV lesions is not generally seen in the immunosuppressed, resulting in severe, persistent and extensive manifestations of HPV disease.
The presence of lymphangiectasis of the thyroid gland.

A branchial cyst is a remnant of embryonic development resulting from a failure of obliteration of a branchial cleft and consists of a subcutaneous cystic mass. Cysts are located anterior or posterior to the ear or in the submandibular region.
Unilateral underdevelopment of the facial tissues, including muscles and bones.
An abnormality of the lacrimal duct, a duct that drain tears from the conjunctiva, via the lacrimal puncta, into the lacrimal sac.

An abnormality of the middle-ear ossicles (three small bones called malleus, incus, and stapes) that are contained within the middle ear and serve to transmit sounds from the air to the fluid-filled labyrinth (cochlea).
A reduction below the normal ratio of the volume of red blood cells to the total volume of blood.
A growth pattern that displays an abnormal difference between the left and the right side.
An increased concentration of isoleucine in the blood.
An increased concentration of leucine in the blood.
Synostosis affecting only one of the coronal sutures.
Shortening of the middle parts of the arm in relation to the upper and terminal segments.

Missing or malformed long bones of the extremities with the distal parts (such as hands and/or feet) connected to the variably shortened or even absent extremity, leading to a flipper-like appearance, as opposed to other forms of limb malformations were either the hole limb is missing (such as amelia), or the distal part of a limb is absent (peromelia).
An anomaly of the joint that connects the upper and the lower arm.
Phocomelia involving all four extremities.
Progressively worsening joint contractures.
The presence of a characteristic high-pitched cry that sounds similar to the meowing of a kitten.
A structural abnormality of the sperm tail.
A structural abnormality of the sperm head.
A persistent cough, defined as a cough lasting longer than eight weeks in adults or longer than four weeks in children.
Concentration of glutamate in the blood circulation above the upper limit of normal.
An increased concentration of ammonia in the blood with sudden onset.
An increased concentration of glutamine in the blood.
Repeated occurrences of acute noninflammatory encephalopathy and fatty degenerative liver failure.
A reduced concentration of copper in the blood.
Concentration of hepcidin in the blood circulation above the upper limit of normal.
Inflammation of the large airways in the lung including any part of the bronchi from the primary bronchi to the tertiary bronchi.
A severe delay in the acquisition of the ability to understand the speech of others.
Excessive, increased hair growth located in the sacral region.
EEG with sharp slow waves in the frontal region. Sharp slow waves are focal sharp transient waves of a duration between 80 and 200 msec followed by a slow wave.
Amount of 3-hydroxypropionic acid in the urine above the upper limit of normal.
Amount of 2-methylcitric acid in the urine above the upper limit of normal.

A congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries with a ventricular septal defect: a hole between the two bottom chambers (ventricles) of the heart. The ventricular septal defect is centered around the most superior aspect of the ventricular septum.

A type of myoclonus in which the myoclonias shift from body region to another in a random and asynchronous fashion. Erratic myoclonus can affect the face or limbs, are brief, single or repetitive, very frequent and nearly continuous.
A chronic loss of joint motion in metacarpophalangeal joints due to structural changes in muscle, tendons, ligaments, or skin that prevents normal movement.
Delayed myelination in the peripheral nervous system.
Nonmidline cleft palate on the left and right sides.
A chronic loss of wrist joint motion on the right and left sides.
Reduced ability to transform factor X into its activated form factor Xa.
Developmental hypoplasia of the primary teeth.
Abnormality of the female genital system.
No identifiable superior and/or inferior lacrimal punctum.
A type of hypothyroidism that results from a defect in the thyroid gland.
Partial or total incontinence of bowel or bladder.
Pneumothorax occurring without traumatic injury to the chest or lung.
An abnormality of the intrahepatic bile duct.

Cholangiocarcinoma is a primary cancer originating in the biliary epithelium i.e., the cholangiocytes, of the extrahepatic and intrahepatic biliary ducts. It is extremely invasive, develops rapidly, often metastasizes, and has a very poor prognosis. They are slow growing tumors which spread longitudinally along the bile ducts with neural, perineural and subepithelial extension.
An increased amount of beta-aminoisobutyric acid in the urine. Beta-aminoisobutyric acid is a non-protein amino acid originating from the catabolism of thymine and valine.
Any anomaly in the function of thrombocytes.
Bleeding sufficiently severe as to require red cell transfusion (WHO Grade 3 or 4).

A common, benign skin condition involving hypertrophy of the sebaceous glands characterized by single or multiple lesions that manifest as yellow, soft, small papules with umbilication. The lesions are located commonly on the central face (specifically, the nose, cheeks and forehead) but may also occur elswehere, including the chest, mouth, scrotum, foreskin, penile shaft, vulva, and areola.

A small benign fibrovascular tumor of the dermal part of the hair disk. Trichodiscoma is rather simple in appearance and consists of a dome-shaped fibrous tumor with a prominent vascular component that fills the papillary dermis under an atrophic epidermis. As in a normal hair disk, a hair follicle may be present at one edge of the papular lesion.
The presence of leiomyoma of the skin.
The presence of multiple lung cysts.

The presence of a piece lung tissue which is not attached to the pulmonary blood supply and does not communicate with the other lung tissue (not connected to the standard bronchial airways and not performing a function in respiration).
The presence of a medullary carcinoma of the thyroid gland.
The presence of multiple polyps in the large intestine.
The presence of leiomyosarcoma of the skin.

Fibrofolliculoma is a clinically asymptomatic, 2-4 mm, skin-colored, dome-shaped smooth papule. It usually arises in the form of multiple lesions in adults in different areas such as the scalp, forehead, face, and neck. According to histology, the lesion is a fibrotic hamartoma characterized by infundibular epithelial proliferation and perifollicular fibrous proliferation.
Structural abnormality of the basal ganglia related to defective development.
Polymicrogyria affecting one or multiple small areas of the cerebral cortex.
Ringed creases of the skin of the extremities related to folding of excess skin.
Spontaneous, repetitive electrical activity demonstrated by electromyography (EMG).
Osteomyelitis of the lower jaw.

An abnormally increased proportion of nuclei of sarcomeres with an internal localization. Individual muscle fibers are syncytia, formed by embryonic fusion of many myoblasts or later, myosatellite cells. Each muscle fiber contains many nuclei, peripherally positioned immediately adjacent to the sarcolemmal membrane. In healthy muscle only 3-5% of fibers contain nuclei that are located internally, within the cell, but many disease processes lead to internal nuclei.
The presence of an abnormally increased amount of connective tissue.
An elevation in bone density of the cortex of one or more diaphyses. Sclerosis is normally detected on a radiograph as an area of increased opacity.
An acute leukemia characterized by the proliferation of both neutrophil and monocyte precursors.
Anemia with varying degrees of erythrocytic hypoplasia without leukopenia or thrombocytopenia.
An abnormality of macrophages.
Congenital lack, i.e., aplasia of the diaphragm.
Abnormal development of the adrenal gland.
A congenital absence or considerable underdevelopment of the trachea such that communication between the larynx proximally and the alveoli of the lungs distally is lacking.
A bony defect in the skull base.
A fissure in the gingiva (gums), i.e., the mucosal tissue that lies over the mandible and maxilla.
A non-midline cleft of the upper lip on one side only.
This term groups together three conditions that presumably represent different degrees of severity of a midline defect of the nose or nasal tip.
Hypopnea is referring to breathing that is abnormally shallow.
An abnormality of the tonsils.
Craniosynostosis involving at least 2 cranial sutures, where the exact pattern of sutures fused has not been precisely specified.
Ingrowth of new blood vessels into the cornea.
Failure to develop of the tricuspid valve and thus lack of the normal connection between the right atrium and the right ventricle.
A structural anomaly of the two central microtubules of motile cilia with a 9+2 microtubuluar configuration.
Delayed tooth eruption affecting the primary dentition.
Nystagmus consisting of horizontal to-and-fro eye movements, in which the movement in one direction is faster than in the other.
Atresia of the biliary tree.
Demyelination of peripheral motor nerves.
Bidirectional ventricular tachycardia (BDVT) is a regular ventricular tachyarrhythmia (VT) with two different QRS morphologies alternating at a rate typically between 140 and 180 bpm.

A longer than normal interval (corrected for heart rate) between the Q and T waves in the heart's cycle. Prolonged QTc can cause premature action potentials during late phase depolarizations thereby leading to ventricular arrhythmias and ventricular fibrillations.
A type of ventricular tachycardia that is characterized by variable QRS complexes within each lead (i.e., QRS complexes may be different from beat to beat).
Increased width of the midpoint of the mandible (mental protuberance) and overlying soft tissue.
Any deviation from the normal concentration of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol in the blood circulation.

Abnormal appearance of the acetabulum characterized by spurs at the medial and lateral acetabular margin and in the center of the acetabulum, giving rise to shape resembling a three-pronged spear sadi to resemble a trident.
A decreased amount of enamel mineralization. Hypomineralized enamel has a brown discoloration and brittle aspect.
A form of hypomineralization of enamel characterized by a chalky appearance of the enamel with orange, brown, or white color.
A reduction in diameter of the distal phalanx of finger towards the distal end.
Bending or curvature of a finger toward the ulnar side (i.e., away from the thumb). The deviation is at the metacarpal-phalangeal joint, and this finding is distinct from clinodactyly.
An abnormality of the appearance of the face caused by constant contraction of the lips leading to a puckered or pursed appearance.
Overgrowth of only one side of the body.

Pronuclei formation is a critical process during fertilisation. Normally, there are two pronuclei (2PN), including the paternal pronucleus and the maternal pronucleus, in the zygote after fertilisation. It is generally accepted that multiple pronuclei (MPN) formation is due to the abnormal extrusion of the second polar body or to abnormal fertilisation with multiple sperm. The MPN therefore can cause infertility and recurrent failure of IVF/ICSI.
Diffuse slowing of cerebral electrical activity recorded along the scalp by electroencephalography (EEG).
EEG with focal sharp transient waves of a duration between 80 and 200 msec followed by a slow wave.
Percussion-induced, local prolonged contractions (mounding) in muscle persisting for several seconds.

A diffusion abnormality observed in diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain. Molecular diffusion refers to the notion that any type of molecule in a fluid (eg, water) is randomly displaced as the molecule is agitated by thermal energy. Restricted diffusion of water appears bright on diffusion-weighted images.
A carcinoma of the larynx.
Premature loss of the permanent teeth.
Localized thickening and tightness of the skin of the fingers or toes.
A form of hyperkeratosis characterized by thickening of the cornified layer without retained nuclei.

A malignant tumor arising from epithelial cells. Carcinomas that arise from glandular epithelium are called adenocarcinomas, those that arise from squamous epithelium are called squamous cell carcinomas, and those that arise from transitional epithelium are called transitional cell carcinomas (NCI Thesaurus).
Absence of the distal phalanges of the toes.
Developmental aplasia of the middle phalanx of third toe.
Atrophy of the capillary lamina of choroid.
An abnormal irregularity of cortical bone.

Abnormally anterior positioning of the infraorbital and perialar regions, or increased convexity of the face, or increased nasolabial angle. The midface includes the maxilla, the cheeks, the zygomas, and the infraorbital and perialar regions of the face
An abnormal increase in the level of lipoprotein cholesterol in the blood.

Eruptive xanthomas are yellow-orange-to-red-brown papules that are often surrounded by an erythematous halo. They appear in crops on the buttocks, extensor surfaces of the extremities, and flexural creases. Acutely, variable amounts of pruritus and pain occur.

A creamy appearance of the retinal blood vessels that occurs when the concentration of lipids in the blood are extremely increased, with pale pink to milky white retinal vessels and altered pale reflexes from choroidal vasculature.

Repeated headache attacks lasting 4-72 h fulfilling at least two of the following criteria: 1) unilateral location, 2) pulsating quality, 3) moderate or severe pain intensity, and 4) aggravation by or causing avoidance of routine physical activity such as climbing stairs. Headache attacks are commonly accompanied by nausea, vomiting, photophobia, or phonophobia.
An increased concentration of 4-hydroxy-L-proline in the urine.
Level of proline in the urine anove the upper limit of normal.
An increased concentration of hydroxyproline in the blood.
The presence of autoantibodies in the serum that react against proteins predominantly expressed in cytoplasmic granules of neutrophils.
Enlargement of lymph nodes surrounding the trachea.
Erythema (redness of the skin caused by hyperemia in superficial capillaries) in the region surrounding a fingernail or toe nail.
A full-thickness defect of the nasal septum.
Underdevelopment or absence of the nose or parts thereof.
Congenital absence (aplasia) of one or more limbs.
Amelia of all four limbs.
A structural anomaly of a male reproductive cell.

Startle-induced seizures are triggered by multiple and non-specific stimuli (auditory, somatosensory, and rarely visual) and are characterized by their sudden unexpected nature. Sudden noise rather than pure sound is the most effective acoustic stimulus.
An abnormal gyral pattern characterized by abnormalities of sulcal depth or orientation.
Excessive number of small gyri (convolutions) on the surface of one side of the brain.
The presence of developmental dysplasia of the cortex of frontal lobe and the cortex of parietal lobe.
An anomaly of the internal capsule, which is an area of white matter in the brain that separates the caudate nucleus and the thalamus from the putamen and the globus pallidus.
Underdevelopment of the right-sided structures of the heart.

The lysosomal-vacuolar pathway has a role in the controlled intracellular digestion of macromolecules such as protein complexes and organelles. This feature refers to the presence of an abnormally increased number of autophagic vacuoles in muscle tissue.
Bowing (abnormal curvature) of the vocal folds.
An abnormality of any of the muscles of the pharynx.
A progressive form of ptosis.
An anomaly of a muscle that is innervated by the facial nerve (the seventh cranial nerve).
An abnormality of an orbicularis oris muscle.
An abnormality of a masseter muscle.

It is estimated that about 40-70 percent of human embryos produced in vitro fertilization (IVF) and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) are viable embryos, whereas others arrest at different early stages of development. The phenotype of preimplantation lethality is inferred if IVF and ICSI cycles fail because all of an individual's embryos are arrested at early stages of development.

Reduced functionality of the process in which a precursor cell type acquires the specialized features of a B cell. A B cell is a lymphocyte of B lineage with the phenotype CD19-positive and capable of B cell mediated immunity.
Swelling of the hand at the knuckles, that gives the fingers a spindle shape (i.e., a round stick with tapered end and a broader base).
Underdevelopment of the alveolar process (also known as alveolar bone).
A cystic lesion originating within the brain.
Any defect in the valve connecting the heart and the pulmonary artery.
A reduction in the size of nerve terminals.
An abnormal reduction in the amplitude of the miniature endplate potentials, i.e. the postsynaptic response to transmitter released from an individual vesicle at the neuromuscular junction.

A type of weakness of a skeletal muscle in the neck that occurs after a muscle group is used and lessens if the muscle group has some rest. That is, there is diminution of strength with repetitive muscle actions.
Reduced ability to flex the femur, that is, to pull the knee upward.
A severe degree of photosensitivity of the skin.
An abnormal enlargement (i.e. increase in measured voltage) of somatosensory evoked potentials.
An intraneuronal inclusion body composed of acid mucopolysaccharides.

A seizure characterized by elementary visual hallucinations such as flashing or flickering lights/colours, or other shapes, simple patterns, scotomata, or amaurosis as its first clinical manifestation.
An anomaly of the dynein arms of motile cilia. This feature is usually appreciated by electron microscopy.
An abnormal high amount of bleeding following the procedure of taking a blood sample.
An abnormally increased degree of bleeding following a superfical injury to the surface of the skin.
A duplication of the renal pelvis.
A tumor (abnormal growth of tissue) of the nervous system.
Failure of the gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) stimulation test to induce an appropriate increased in luteinizing hormone (LH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels.
A type of tumor of the pancreatic beta cells that secretes excess insulin and can result in hypoglycemia.
The presence of multiple pancreatic islet cell adenomas.
Intermittent abdominal pain with diarrhea and/or constipation.
Abnormality of the temporal bone of the skull, which is situated at the sides and base of the skull roughly underlying the region of the face known as the temple.
Ultra-low vision but with retained ability to identify a moving object (typically hand motion at distance of 30 cm).
A congenital form of torticollis resulting from shortening of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and leading to a limited range of motion in both rotation and lateral bending.
In otosclerosis, a callus of bone accumulates on the stapes creating a partial fixation. This limits the movement of the stapes bone, which results in hearing loss.
Fissure within the spinal cord of the neck.
Sudden and involuntary contractions of one or more muscles brought on by physical exertion.
An abnormal increase in the amount of intramuscular fat tissue.
Sudden and involuntary contractions of one or more muscles brought on by exposure to cold temperatures.
Pain of the gastrocnemius muscle.
A histological phenotype observed on testicular biopsy in which only Sertoli cells line the seminiferous tubules of the testis.
An abnormality of the fetus or the birth of the fetus, excluding structural abnormalities.
Abnormally small dimension of the mandible (lower jaw) relative to the maxilla (upper jaw).

Trichorrhexis nodosa is the formation of nodes along the hair shaft through which breakage readily occurs. It is thus a focal defect in the hair fiber that is characterized by thickening or weak points (nodes) that cause the hair to break off easily. The result is defective, abnormally fragile hair.
Placement of the nipples at a lower than normal location.
Lack of subcutaneous adipose tissue.
A spasm (sudden, involuntary constriction) of the bronchioles.
Fibrous bands (i.e., bands of scar-like tissue) that span two or more intra-abdominal organs and/or the inner abdominal wall (i.e. peritoneal membrane).
Weakness of both lower extremities with sparing of the upper extremities. Paraplegia refers to a severe or complete loss of strength, whereas paraparesis refers to a relatively mild loss of strength.

A reduced ability to participate in the back-and-forth flow of social interaction appropriate to culture and developmental level, which is normally characterized by an influence of the behavior of one person on the behavior of another person.
An abnormal appearance of hair under polarizing microscopy (using crossed polarizers), whereby hair shafts show striking alternating bright and dark bands, often referred to as tiger tail banding.
An elevation over the normal range of the average amount of hemoglobin per red blood cell (27 to 31 picograms/cell).
A nail plate that has a longitudinal separation and the two sections of the nail share the same lateral radius of curvature.
Inspiratory stridor is a high pitched sound upon inspiration that is generally related to laryngeal abnormalities.

A hazy area of increased attenuation in centrilobular areas of the lung with preserved bronchial and vascular markings seen on a computer tomography scan. Centrilobular refers to a location that is central within secondary pulmonary lobules.
The presence of blood in the pleural space.
An abnormally elevated blood pressure in the circulation of the pulmonary artery.
Presence of thickening of the interlobular septa of the lungs as seen on a CT scan.
Substantial narrowing or blockage of small pulmonary veins as a result of disorganized smooth muscle hypertrophy and collagen matrix deposition.
Temporally uniform (all lesions are in the same stage of evolution) pattern of diffuse inflammatory interstitial process, mostly symmetric over the entire lung, involving mainly the alveolar septa.

Intralobular septal thickening is a computed tomography finding of increased width of the walls (septa) within a pulmonary lobule. Secondary pulmonary lobules represent a cluster of up to 30 acini 9 supplied by a common distal pulmonary artery and bronchiole. These clustered acini are bounded by interstitial fibrous septa (interlobular septa) which outline an irregular polyhedron of varying size between 1 and 2.5 cm. Interlobular septal thickening is seen on chest radiographs as thin linear opacities at right angles to and in contact with the lateral pleural surfaces near the lung bases. In contrast, intralobular septal thickening are visible as fine linear opacities in a lobule when the intralobular interstitial tissue is abnormally thickened. When numerous, they may appear as a fine reticular pattern.

Usually, Neutrophils make up less than 3% of all cells found in the broncho-alveloar lavage fluid. In children, standard value of neutrophils is higher depending on their age (children under the age of 5 show a maximum value of 10%). This elevated cell proportion is a sign for acute and chronic infections (HP:0012387, HP:0006538) and can be associated to specific diseases.

Usually, eosinophils make up less than 0.5% of all cells found in the broncho-alveloar lavage fluid. But in eosinophilic lung disease, the eosinophil cell proportion typically represents more than 25%. Comment: An elevated level of eosinophil cells are also a result of infections, or an allergic reaction or can be drug-induced.
Thick, elongated, worm-like or corkscrew eosinophilic bundle that are found on H&E staining of the brain in the presence of long standing gliosis, occasional tumors, and some metabolic disorders.

Fusion involving two or more metacarpal bones (A synostosis of the first metacarpal and the proximal phalanx of the thumb can also be observed, note that the first metacarpal bone corresponds to a proximal phalanx).
Absence or underdevelopment of the big toe.
Fusion of two or more phalangeal bones of the hand.
Fusion of the proximal and middle phalanges of the 5th finger.
Absence or underdevelopment (hypoplasia) of the middle phalanx of the little (5th) finger.
Absence or underdevelopment of the ulna.
Adenocarcinoma of the Bronchus.
An increased concentration of 2-hydroxyglutaric acid in the urine.
A form of anomalous pulmonary venous return in which not all pulmonary veins drain abnormally. Partial anomalous pulmonary venous return frequently involves one or both of the veins from one lung.

A type of heterotaxy where some paired structures on opposite sides of the left-right axis of the body are symmetrical mirror images of each other, and have the morphology of the normal left-sided structures.

The essence of the lesion is the combination of discordant atrioventricular and ventriculo-arterial connections. Thus, the morphologically right atrium is connected to a morphologically left ventricle across the mitral valve, with the left ventricle then connected to the pulmonary trunk. The morphologically left atrium is connected to the morphologically right ventricle across the tricuspid valve, with the morphologically right ventricle connected to the aorta.
The condition in which both atria are joined to the right ventricle each by its own atrioventricular valve. Usually, the left ventricle is hypoplastic.
Connection of the right atrium to the left ventricle and of the left atrium to the right ventricle in a biventricular heart.

Abnormal increase in blood pressure. An individual measurement of increased blood pressure does not necessarily imply hypertension. In practical terms, multiple measurements are recommended to diagnose the presence of hypertension.
An abnormality of the tragus.
Increased width of the femoral head.
A discontinuity of the vertebral arch, i.e., of the posterior part of a vertebra.
Presence of abnormal convexity of the upper and lower end plates of the vertebrae, i.e., an exaggerated bulging out of the upper and lower vertebral end plates.
Partial duplication of the first metacarpal bone.
An anomaly of the color of the nail.
Absence or underdevelopment of the femur.
Chronic reduction in active and passive mobility of the shoulder joint due to structural changes in muscle, tendons, ligaments, or skin that prevents normal movement.
This term refers to the loss of eyelashes that were previously present.
An anomaly of the the pubic bone, i.e., of the ventral and anterior of the three principal components (pubis, ilium, ischium) of the hip bone.

Severe microcephaly and lissencephaly with granular surfaces with immature cortical plate, reduced in thickness, with focal polymicrogyria and immature small neurons with rare processes, intermingled with a considerable number of glial elements.
A structural abnormality of a skeletal muscle.
An abnormality of the nasal septum.
